Summary
Welcome to CPSC 221 — Data Structures and Algorithms! In this course we will learn to design and evaluate programmatic approaches to problem solving. The course has 3 main units. Though they overlap and influence one another, we will address the units in roughly this order:

reasoning about code
classic data structures
graph algorithms

Today’s lesson is an introduction to the context in which we evaluate our code, and the issues we consider when we do so.

title: Syllabus
text:
CPSC 221 teaches you to design, implement, and analyze the classic data structures and algorithms of computer science — and to reason rigorously about when and why to use them. You’ll come away able to:

Define and articulate the functionality of classic data structures such as stacks, queues, dictionaries, and priority queues by their Abstract Data Type (ADT).
Design algorithms and structures to implement novel ADTs based on properties of the data and intended use.
Implement classic and novel data structures in modern C++, including arrays, linked lists, AVL trees, and hash tables.
Analyze the efficiency (time and space) of algorithms and data structures using asymptotic notation.
Justify algorithmic choices using iterative and recursive proofs of correctness.
Evaluate asymptotic time and space tradeoffs between implementation options.
Identify the structures and algorithms necessary for solving complex problems.
Synthesize and apply algorithmic and analytical design choices to form complete software solutions to classic problems.

Programming assignments and homework are project-like: you (and an optional partner) manage your own progress within a 1–2 week work window, and assignments may overlap. Labs are weekly coding exercises auto-graded on PrairieLearn; your 8 highest lab scores (of 10) count toward your grade. Examlets are (nearly) weekly, self-scheduled, and focus on the previous week’s content — practice material includes old exams and PrairieLearn practice problems.

Collaboration policy
Some assignments allow groups of up to 2; others require independent work. For homework and most programming assignments, you may work with at most one partner — but each student must submit their own copy, even if it’s identical to their partner’s.
The point of every assignment is to learn new things and develop skills. Copying a partner’s work, or splitting an assignment in half so each of you only does part of it, means you gain nothing from it — and since assignments carry much less weight than the examlets and final, that lack of practice will show up on the exams that actually determine your grade.
A better approach: do as much on your own as you can, and talk things over with others when you get stuck. Struggling through your own mistakes until you solve a problem teaches the material far better than being told the answer.


Generative AI policy
You are free to use generative AI tools (ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, etc.) on Programming Assignments, Homework, and Labs, without restriction — but please briefly cite their use in a code comment where you used them (e.g. // used Claude to help debug this function). If you’re working with a coding agent, you can just ask it to add that disclosure comment for you.
We take this approach because we do not want to spend valuable teaching and learning time trying to detect AI use on take-home work. We believe that you are curious and energetic, and this material is fun to master, so we leave it to you to decide how best to learn it.
That said: the entire point of the PAs, HWs, and Labs is to build understanding you can draw upon independently and fluently. Your understanding, fluency, and expertise will be assessed under invigilated conditions (at ORCA) on the examlets and final exam, which together are worth 80% of your grade. AI will not be available on any CPSC221 assessment in ORCA.
See also UBC’s 10 things UBC students should know about generative AI.


Textbooks
There is no required textbook. Lecture and practice material should be sufficient, but if you’d like a reference:

Discrete Mathematics with Applications (Epp)
Data Abstraction & Problem Solving with C++: Walls and Mirrors (Carrano)

Earlier editions, or textbooks from different authors, work fine too — we’ll be clear about the topics we’re covering so you can find them in any resource. A good C++ reference is a necessity; cppreference.com and learncpp.com are both solid.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Asymptotic notation
For positive constants \(c\) and \(n_0\):








\(T(n) \in O(f(n))\)
if \(\exists\, c, n_0\) such that
\(T(n) \le c\,f(n)\) for all \(n \ge n_0\)


\(T(n) \in \Omega(f(n))\)
if \(\exists\, c, n_0\) such that
\(T(n) \ge c\,f(n)\) for all \(n \ge n_0\)


\(T(n) \in \Theta(f(n))\)
if
\(T(n) \in O(f(n))\) and \(T(n) \in \Omega(f(n))\)


\(T(n) \in o(f(n))\)
if for any \(c\), \(\exists\, n_0\) such that
\(T(n) < c\,f(n)\) for all \(n \ge n_0\)


\(T(n) \in \omega(f(n))\)
if for any \(c\), \(\exists\, n_0\) such that
\(T(n) > c\,f(n)\) for all \(n \ge n_0\)




The whole family on one page, for reference rather than for working through.
The distinction worth thirty seconds if anyone asks: \(O\) and \(\Omega\) say there exists a constant; \(o\) and \(\omega\) say for every constant. That is why little-o is strictly stronger than big-O – no constant, however generous, saves you.
They will need \(\Omega\) and \(\Theta\) on the examlet and in PEX1. This slide is where they come from; the practice questions are where they get learned.

title: CPSC 221
text:
The invariant
We want, at exit: retloc is the index of the min of C[a..n-1].


So carry that claim through the loop:



Loop invariant. At the start of iteration \(i\), retloc is the index of the minimum value in C[a..___].




The blank is i-1, and the whole exercise is getting it right.
At the top of iteration \(i\) we have not yet examined C[i], so the range we can vouch for stops at \(i-1\). Almost everyone writes a..i.
Check it against the exit: the loop ends with \(i = n\), so the invariant reads C[a..n-1] – exactly the theorem. That is the test for whether you chose the right invariant, and it is worth doing out loud: a good invariant is one that becomes the theorem when the loop stops.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Proof Strategy



Loop invariant. At the start of iteration \(i\), retloc is the index of the minimum value in C[a..___].



Proving the Theorem requires three things:








Initialization
the invariant is true before the first iteration


Restoration
if true at the start of iteration \(i\), it is true at the start of \(i+1\)


Termination
the loop ends — and invariant + exit condition give the theorem






What does this smell like?

Say “this is induction” out loud. Initialization is the base case, maintenance is the inductive step. They have the machinery from 121; naming it means they can reuse it instead of learning a ritual.
Termination is the part that is not induction and the part they forget. It is where the invariant gets cashed in.

title: CPSC 221

text:
The recipe








1. Recognize the Claim
the postcondition you are trying to reach


2. Find an invariant
strong enough to give that at exit, and still true after one pass


3. Initialization
true before the first iteration


4. Restoration
start of \(i\) \(\Rightarrow\) start of \(i{+}1\)


5. Termination
the loop ends, and invariant gives result






Here the invariant was the theorem with \(n\) replaced by \(i\). That is the easy case — often it has to say more than the theorem.


Proving correctness is only one use of invariants — they are also how you design a loop in the first place.

Steps 1 and 2 are the ones this lecture added. Most students arrive able to do 3, 4, 5 mechanically and with no idea where the invariant came from.
Do not oversell step 2. idxOfMin is the easy case, where the invariant is the theorem with \(n\) replaced by \(i\). In general the invariant must be stronger than the postcondition, because a claim that barely implies the result will not survive an iteration – binary search carries “if q is present it is in [lo,hi]”, Euclid carries gcd(x,y) unchanged, the playlist partition carries three moving boundaries. None of those is the theorem with a substitution.
That is strengthening the induction hypothesis, which they saw in 121. Worth naming if someone asks why their invariant will not go through – usually it is too weak, not wrong.
Land the last line. An invariant written before the body tells you what the body must do; written after, it is an audit. The first is the more valuable habit – and it is what HW1 zone 3 is actually asking for.

title: Setup: Tech stack
text:
Computing environment
All programming assignments and labs in this course use C++, compiled with clang. You submit your .h/.cpp files directly to PrairieLearn, which compiles and tests them for you — but you’ll want a working local (or remote) build to develop and debug against before you submit.

Connect to the department’s remote server
The department provides a shared Linux server for coursework: remote.students.cs.ubc.ca, accessible via SSH with your CWL ID and password (not a separate CS account).
Recommended: VS Code + Remote-SSH

Download VS Code.
Install the Remote - SSH extension (search “SSH - Remote” in the Extensions panel).
Click the new remote-connection icon in the bottom-left corner, choose Add New SSH Host, and enter your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca.
If prompted for a platform, choose Linux (the remote servers run Linux, regardless of your own OS).
Connect, enter your CWL password, then use the Files Explorer to open a folder — this becomes your working directory on the server.

To skip re-entering your password every time, generate an SSH key and copy it to the server:
ssh-keygen
ssh-copy-id your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca   # macOS/Linux
(On Windows, use type path\to\id_rsa.pub | ssh your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca "cat >> .ssh/authorized_keys" instead of ssh-copy-id.)


The command line
You’ll be working at a Linux shell on the remote server. If you’re new to it:
pwd            # print working directory
ls             # list files in the current folder
cd FOLDER      # change into FOLDER; cd .. goes up, cd (no args) goes home
mkdir FOLDER   # create a folder
rm FILE        # delete FILE; rm -r FOLDER deletes a folder and its contents
mv SRC DEST    # move/rename
cp SRC DEST    # copy
make PROGRAM   # build PROGRAM using the rules in a Makefile


Getting lab/assignment files onto the server
Each lab/PA is distributed as a .zip from PrairieLearn. Get it onto the server with either:

VS Code: drag and drop the unzipped folder into the Files Explorer once connected, or
Command line (macOS/Linux): scp your-file.zip your-CWL-id@remote.students.cs.ubc.ca:path/to/folder, then ssh in and unzip your-file.zip.



Compiling and testing
Most labs/PAs include a Makefile. To build:
make
If make fails, read the error message — clang is generally good about pointing at what’s wrong and suggesting a fix. If it succeeds, run the resulting executable directly (e.g. ./lab_intro) to test your work before submitting.
Submission is separate from compiling locally: you upload your source files to the PrairieLearn question, which compiles and grades them independently. A clean local build is a good sign, but the PrairieLearn autograder result is what counts.


C++ references

cplusplus.com and cppreference.com — language/standard library references
Unix and make/Makefile tutorials — the lab starter code builds with make, so a basic understanding of Makefiles will help
If you’re coming from Java: search for “C++ for Java programmers” guides to map concepts you already know onto C++ syntax



C++ short course (optional)
A past offering of this course recorded an optional video series introducing C++ specifically for this course’s needs (classes, pointers, arrays, parameter passing, the “Big 3,” operator overloading). See the C++ Short Course page for the recordings and slides.


More tips and optional readings
The older Computing Environment page has additional background on the department’s servers (it predates the current remote.students.cs.ubc.ca hostname, but the general concepts still apply).

title: Lesson plan — What Does It Do?
text:
Students should feel, in their own mouths, that a sentence they were confident about does not survive being said out loud — and then watch the room build a correct one together in twenty minutes, from nothing but conversation.
The lesson is not “you all failed” and it is not “AI will ruin you.” The arc is generous on purpose:

Individually, almost nobody writes a precise description.
Through conversation, almost everybody gets there.
Therefore: the conversation was the thing that worked.

That last step is the argument for being in the room, and it is demonstrated rather than asserted — which matters, because attendance is not required in this course and the lesson must not quietly contradict that.

title: Lesson plan — What Does It Do?
section: The three moves that make this work
text:
The three moves that make this work

1. Simultaneous reading, not round-robin
Everybody reads their own statement aloud at the same time, whole room, about thirty seconds. This is better than taking turns for four reasons: no performance anxiety among strangers in week 1, every single student actually does it, no confident voice anchors the group before others have spoken, and it is fast.
The purpose is for the speaker to hear themselves, not for anyone else to listen. Say that explicitly — “nobody is listening to you, that’s the point.”
Tell them twice not to fix the sentence as they read it. Students patch their own wording mid-sentence automatically, half a second before they reach the gap, and it destroys the entire effect. Naming it is the only defence.
Afterwards, ask “did it sound like you expected?” and wait. Laughter and groans here are the lesson landing.


2. An adjudication test, not a vote
“Whose is correct?” needs a criterion or groups just pick the one that sounds nicest:

Could a stranger reimplement this function correctly, from these words alone?



3. You play the pedantic genie
Take real statements from the room and satisfy them legally but wrongly. Playful, not punitive — you are a malicious implementer, not a judge.







Their words
What you hand back




“finds the key in the list”
Returns true. I found it.


“returns the position of the key”
[5,3,5], key 5 → returns 2. Also a position.


“returns the index of the key”
Key absent → returns 0. You didn’t say.


“returns where the key is”
A 1-based index. You didn’t say.


“searches for the key and returns it”
Returns 5. You said return it.


“returns the index of the key, or -1”
Returns any matching index. You never said first.



That last row is the important one: it catches students who were already being careful, so nobody in the room gets to feel exempt.

title: Lesson plan — What Does It Do?
text:
Watch for: transcription
Someone will narrate the code instead of describing it — “it loops from 0 to size, and if arr[i] equals q it returns i.” That technically passes the reimplementation test, which makes it a good ninety seconds if it comes up naturally: it tells you what the code says, never what it is for, and it is no shorter than just reading the code.
The giveaway is the blank in the function name. A transcription cannot name the function; a real description hands you the name almost for free.
Keep this in your pocket rather than on a slide — take it only if a student raises it.

title: Lesson plan — What Does It Do?
text:
The naming payoff
“Find” was never enough — a function called find could return a bool, a value, or an iterator. A precise description yields indexOfFirst / firstIndexOf almost automatically. Use this to fill in the blanked-out name.

title: Lesson plan — What Does It Do?
section: The AI moment — generate it live
text:
The AI moment — generate it live
Paste the function into whichever tool you like, in front of them, and let the room watch it produce a clean, correct description in about three seconds. Live is far better than a screenshot: it is more honest, it removes any suspicion of cherry-picking, and the speed is the point.
It will be correct. Do not pretend otherwise — the lesson does not depend on AI being wrong, and students will disengage instantly if you overstate it.
The line that matters:

You are nodding, because it looks right. You would have nodded twenty minutes ago too — before you knew what you were missing.

Then: recognizing a correct answer and being able to produce one feel identical from the inside, and only one of them is what an examlet tests.

title: Lesson plan — What Does It Do?
text:
The closing contract
Three people who just succeeded together agree on one shared phrase:

“Say that more precisely.”

Aimed at the practice, not the relationship — so it costs nothing personal, requires no exchange of contact details, and works on a partner, a TA, a future study group, or yourself.
Then start using it from the front of the room constantly, all term. Heard in week 1 and then every week after, it stops being an event and becomes how this course talks.

On the optional contact swap
Offer it, then say “or nothing at all” clearly and move on fast.
In a room this size there will be a few students with real reasons not to hand their number to two people they met twenty minutes ago. If the whole room is exchanging while you watch, declining becomes conspicuous — naming the opt-out out loud is what makes it free.
Collect nothing, build no roster, and do not ask next week who is still meeting. Any follow-up makes the opt-out visible again.

title: Lesson plan — What Does It Do?
text:
Known risks

Some students finish writing in ninety seconds. They are usually the ones about to discover they were imprecise. Hold the full five minutes.
A group agrees immediately and goes quiet. They accepted the first statement without testing it. Nudge: “read me the shortest one and I’ll tell you how I’d break it.”
Tone in the breaking phase. Pedantic genie, not judge. If it reads as mockery in week 1, you lose volunteers for the term.
Do not add an attendance pitch at the end. The students in the room just lived the argument. Saying it out loud a second time cheapens it.

For later: the AI comparison
Cut from this lesson deliberately — a tool producing the sentence in three seconds argues against the point, which is that they needed each other. It belongs in a lecture where assessment is the subject.
Worth keeping when that lecture happens (tested 2026-09-11): asked what the function does, Gemini omitted “first”; ChatGPT got it right. That is the demonstration in one line — the word the whole room fights over is the word a widely-used tool drops, and you cannot tell which you got without already knowing the answer.
A local chat window for doing this live, driven by the claude CLI so no API key is involved, is in tools/aidemo/server.py at the root of the superproject.

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text: Written to be worked at the board. It leans on two results rather than reproving them: idxOfMin, proved in lecture 4/5, and swap, assumed.

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
section: What we are allowed to assume
text:
What we are allowed to assume






Lemma 1 (idxOfMin). For \(0 \le a < n\), idxOfMin(C, a) returns an index \(\ell\) with \(a \le \ell < n\) and \[C[\ell] \;=\; \min_{a \le j < n} C[j],\] and does not modify C.









Lemma 2 (swap). swap(C, p, q) leaves C with \(C'[p] = C[q]\), \(C'[q] = C[p]\), and \(C'[k] = C[k]\) for every \(k \notin \{p, q\}\). In particular it is a transposition, so it permutes the contents of C.

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text:
What we are proving






Theorem. After selectionSort(C) returns, C is a permutation of \(C_0\) and \(C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[n-1]\).



Both halves are needed. Sortedness alone is satisfied by a function that overwrites the array with zeroes.

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text:
The invariant
At the top of iteration \(i\) — meaning just before the guard is tested with the loop variable equal to \(i\) — for \(0 \le i \le n\):






\(P(i)\):

C is a permutation of \(C_0\);
\(C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[i-1]\);
\(\displaystyle\max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]\).




Clauses (b) and (c) are vacuous when \(i = 0\); (c) is also vacuous when \(i = n\).
Clause (c) is the one that does not appear in the theorem. It is carried purely to make the induction go through — see the remark at the end.

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text:
a) Initialization
Take \(i = 0\).

No statement has executed, so C holds \(C_0\), and the identity is a permutation.
The range \(C[0..{-1}]\) is empty, and the empty sequence is sorted.
There is no \(k\) with \(0 \le k < 0\), so the maximum is over an empty set and the claim is vacuous.

Hence \(P(0)\). \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text:
b) Restoration
Assume \(P(i)\) holds at the top of iteration \(i\), and that the guard passed, so \(i < n\). Let C denote the contents at the top of the iteration and \(C'\) the contents after the body runs. We show \(P(i+1)\) holds of \(C'\).
The body does two things:
\[m \;=\; \texttt{idxOfMin(C, i)}, \qquad \texttt{swap(C, m, i)}.\]
By Lemma 1, \(i \le m < n\) and \[C[m] \;=\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j], \tag{$\star$}\] and C is unchanged by the call. By Lemma 2, \[C'[i] = C[m], \qquad C'[m] = C[i], \qquad C'[k] = C[k] \text{ otherwise.}\]
(a) Permutation. idxOfMin does not modify C, and swap is a transposition. A composition of permutations is a permutation, so by the inductive hypothesis \(C'\) is a permutation of \(C_0\).
(b) The prefix is sorted. We must show \(C'[0] \le \cdots \le C'[i]\).
Since \(m \ge i\), the swap touches only indices \(\ge i\), so \[C'[k] = C[k] \quad \text{for all } k < i,\] and by the inductive hypothesis (b) this prefix is sorted. It remains to check the join, that \(C'[i-1] \le C'[i]\), and only when \(i \ge 1\).
By the inductive hypothesis (c), \[C[i-1] \;\le\; \max_{0 \le k < i} C[k] \;\le\; \min_{i \le j < n} C[j]
\;\overset{(\star)}{=}\; C[m] \;=\; C'[i],\] and \(C'[i-1] = C[i-1]\), so \(C'[i-1] \le C'[i]\) as required.
When \(i = 0\) the range \(C'[0..0]\) is a single element and is sorted trivially.
(c) The prefix stays below the suffix. We must show \[\max_{0 \le k < i+1} C'[k] \;\le\; \min_{i+1 \le j < n} C'[j].\]
By part (b) just proved, \(C'[0..i]\) is sorted, so its maximum is its last entry: \[\max_{0 \le k \le i} C'[k] \;=\; C'[i] \;=\; C[m].\]
For the right-hand side, compare the two suffixes as multisets. The swap moves \(C[m]\) to position \(i\) and \(C[i]\) to position \(m\), and both \(i\) and \(m\) lie in \([i, n)\), so \[\{\, C'[j] : i+1 \le j < n \,\} \;=\; \{\, C[j] : i \le j < n \,\} \setminus \{ C[m] \}.\]
Every element of \(\{C[j] : i \le j < n\}\) is \(\ge C[m]\) by \((\star)\), since \(C[m]\) is the minimum of exactly that set. Removing one element cannot introduce anything smaller, so every remaining element is \(\ge C[m] = C'[i]\), which is the claim.
Hence \(P(i+1)\). \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text:
c) Termination
The loop variable starts at \(0\), increases by exactly \(1\) per iteration, and is tested against the fixed bound \(n\). So after \(n\) iterations the guard fails and control leaves the loop with \(i = n\).
\(P(n)\) therefore holds, and reading it off:


C is a permutation of \(C_0\);


\(C[0] \le C[1] \le \cdots \le C[n-1]\) — the whole array is sorted;


vacuous.


Together, (a) and (b) are exactly the theorem. \(\qquad\blacksquare\)

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text:
Remark: why clause (c) is there
Drop (c) and the proof fails at one specific line. In part (b) we needed \(C'[i-1] \le C'[i]\), and the only thing that delivers it is knowing that everything already placed is no larger than anything still to come. Sortedness of the prefix alone says nothing about how the prefix compares to the rest, so the newly placed element could land below its predecessor.
So (c) is not part of what we set out to prove, and it is not used at termination — it retires there, vacuous. It exists solely so that the inductive step can be taken. That is strengthening the induction hypothesis: the statement you can prove is sometimes stronger than the one you want.

title: Selection sort — a formal proof of correctness
text:
Remark: the last iteration
The loop runs to \(i = n-1\), where idxOfMin(C, n-1) must return \(n-1\) and the swap exchanges an element with itself. It is harmless, and the proof covers it without a special case, but the loop could equally run to \(n-2\). Worth a sentence if someone asks — it is the same observation as the final pass of a bubble sort doing nothing.

title: C++ Short Course (optional)

What are the possible values of \(i\)?
Stop the algorithm at some iteration \(i\) — what do we know about the variables?

Pen work on the array. Stop it at \(i = 5\) and ask what retloc must be. Then \(i = 9\). They will get there concretely before they can say it generally, which is the right order.
\(i\) ranges over \(a{+}1 \ldots n{-}1\). The answer you are steering toward: retloc is the index of the smallest element seen so far – and “so far” is the thing that needs pinning down precisely.

title: CPSC 221
section: What are we trying to prove?

title: CPSC 221
text:
The invariant
We want, at exit: retloc is the index of the min of C[a..n-1].


So carry that claim through the loop:



Loop invariant. At the start of iteration \(i\), retloc is the index of the minimum value in C[a..___].




The blank is i-1, and the whole exercise is getting it right.
At the top of iteration \(i\) we have not yet examined C[i], so the range we can vouch for stops at \(i-1\). Almost everyone writes a..i.
Check it against the exit: the loop ends with \(i = n\), so the invariant reads C[a..n-1] – exactly the theorem. That is the test for whether you chose the right invariant, and it is worth doing out loud: a good invariant is one that becomes the theorem when the loop stops.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Proof Strategy



Loop invariant. At the start of iteration \(i\), retloc is the index of the minimum value in C[a..___].



Proving the Theorem requires three things:








Initialization
the invariant is true before the first iteration


Restoration
if true at the start of iteration \(i\), it is true at the start of \(i+1\)


Termination
the loop ends — and invariant + exit condition give the theorem






What does this smell like?

Say “this is induction” out loud. Initialization is the base case, maintenance is the inductive step. They have the machinery from 121; naming it means they can reuse it instead of learning a ritual.
Termination is the part that is not induction and the part they forget. It is where the invariant gets cashed in.

title: CPSC 221

text:
The recipe








1. Recognize the Claim
the postcondition you are trying to reach


2. Find an invariant
strong enough to give that at exit, and still true after one pass


3. Initialization
true before the first iteration


4. Restoration
start of \(i\) \(\Rightarrow\) start of \(i{+}1\)


5. Termination
the loop ends, and invariant gives result






Here the invariant was the theorem with \(n\) replaced by \(i\). That is the easy case — often it has to say more than the theorem.


Proving correctness is only one use of invariants — they are also how you design a loop in the first place.

Steps 1 and 2 are the ones this lecture added. Most students arrive able to do 3, 4, 5 mechanically and with no idea where the invariant came from.
Do not oversell step 2. idxOfMin is the easy case, where the invariant is the theorem with \(n\) replaced by \(i\). In general the invariant must be stronger than the postcondition, because a claim that barely implies the result will not survive an iteration – binary search carries “if q is present it is in [lo,hi]”, Euclid carries gcd(x,y) unchanged, the playlist partition carries three moving boundaries. None of those is the theorem with a substitution.
That is strengthening the induction hypothesis, which they saw in 121. Worth naming if someone asks why their invariant will not go through – usually it is too weak, not wrong.
Land the last line. An invariant written before the body tells you what the body must do; written after, it is an audit. The first is the more valuable habit – and it is what HW1 zone 3 is actually asking for.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Warm-up
My algorithm runs in time \(\Omega(n \log n)\).
Your algorithm runs in time \(O(n!)\).


Whose is better?

The answer is: you cannot tell, and that is the whole point.
Mine is bounded below – it takes at least \(n\log n\), and might take \(n^{100}\). Yours is bounded above – it takes at most \(n!\), and might take constant time. The two claims do not meet, so no comparison follows.
Worth saying plainly on the recording: these are the two bounds pointing in opposite directions, and reading \(\Omega\) as “best case” and \(O\) as “worst case” is what makes people think a comparison is available here.
Pause after the question. Viewers can stop and think.

My code crashed partway through the loop.
What is the latest iteration I could have been on?

This is the best slide in the lecture. Pause here.
Answer: \(i = 3\). How you get there is the point.
The prefix looks sorted a long way – 7, 11, 15, 21, 29 – so the eyeball answer is 5. But 18 is sitting at index 14. For the invariant to hold at \(i=5\) the first five entries would have to be the five smallest, and they are not: 18 belongs in there and 29 does not. Same failure at \(i=4\).
At \(i=3\) it holds: 7, 11, 15 really are the three smallest values in the array, and they are sorted. So iteration 3 had begun and not finished – it would have found 18 and swapped it into position 3.
Two things to land:

The weak invariant cannot answer this. “The prefix is sorted” is true through index 4 and gives the wrong answer. Only “and holds the \(i\) smallest” gets you there – the clause we added one slide ago, doing work.
You just read the state of a crashed program off the data. That is what invariants are for outside of proofs: they say what must be true at any moment, which is exactly what debugging is.

What is always true?
At the start of iteration \(i\):



C[0..i-1] is sorted.





Is that enough?

Take this seriously for a moment – it is the answer everyone gives, and it is true. It is just not enough.
Try restoration with it: assume C[0..i-1] is sorted, run one iteration, and try to conclude C[0..i] is sorted. You cannot. Nothing stops the element we just dropped into position \(i\) from being smaller than C[i-1] – unless we already knew the prefix held the smallest elements.
Let them sit with the failed attempt before the fix. The failure is the lesson.

At the start of iteration \(i\):   C[0..i-1] is sorted, and holds the \(i\) smallest values in C.




This is lecture 4’s closing point, arrived at the hard way: the invariant has to be stronger than the postcondition.
The theorem only says the array ends up sorted. “Holds the \(i\) smallest” never appears in it. But drop that clause and restoration fails, so the proof needs it – carried through every iteration purely to make the induction go.
Name it: strengthening the induction hypothesis. Same move as 121.

If an algorithm is not correct, is its value 0?



No — and the exceptions are important and worth considering:

approximation — provably close, much faster
heuristics — usually good, no promise
randomized — correct with high probability
restricted inputs — correct on the data you actually have

Which of these are you willing to wait for?

Anchor: the universe is about 4.4 x 10^17 seconds old.

10^12 s (n^2 at n=10^12) — ~32,000 years. About 5x all of recorded history; back to the Chauvet cave paintings.
10^18 s (2^n at n=100) — ~32 billion years. 2.3x the age of the universe.
10^24 s (n^3 at n=10^12) — ~32 quadrillion years. 2.3 million x the age of the universe.
10^289 s (2^n at n=1000) — 10^271 x the age of the universe. There are only ~10^80 atoms in the observable universe; this exceeds that by 10^209.

If you only use one line: 2^n at n=100 already outruns the universe. Not a million. A hundred.
Small end: 10^-9 s is one nanosecond, and light travels 30 cm in it – Grace Hopper handed out 11.8-inch wires so engineers would stop asking why satellite calls were slow. At 10^-11 s light travels 3 mm.
Two framings if there is time:

The n^3 row is the scary one. 2^n is easy to dismiss as pathological, but n^3 is an innocent triple loop – and at n=10,000 it is already 1 second while n is still at 10^-8.
Faster hardware does not save you. A machine 1000x faster turns 10^289 into 10^286. The exponential eats all of hardware progress and doesn’t notice. That is why this is a math course, not a benchmarking course.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Example 1, continued
Form groups of size 3. Look at the group papers.
How many written statements can you see in your group?

Quick scan of the room. This is a compliance check that costs ten seconds and requires collecting nothing. Groups police themselves.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Example 1, continued
Read your statement out loud, simultaneously on the count of 3.

don’t fix it as you read! You are going to want to. You will see the gap about half a second before you reach it, and your instinct will be to quietly patch it as you speak.
Resist that. You are reading it so that you can hear it.
Let the whole room read at once – it takes about thirty seconds and the wall of sound is worth having. Two hundred people saying different sentences about the same four lines of code makes the point before anyone discusses anything.
Reading simultaneously does three things a round-robin cannot: it removes all performance anxiety in week 1 among strangers, it guarantees every single student actually does it, and it means no confident voice anchors the group before the others have spoken.
The instruction not to self-repair is the important one. Say it twice. Students patching their own sentences mid-read is automatic and it is exactly what destroys the effect.

title: CPSC 221
text:
Example 1, continued
Share your statements, and discuss them.
Write a final description for your group.

Circulate. Listen for the argument – the groups doing this properly get loud. Silent groups usually accepted the first statement without testing it.
Useful nudge if a group is stuck agreeing: “read me the shortest one, and I’ll tell you how I’d break it.”

CPSC 221
text:
What just happened?

Deliberately bare – this part is talked, not projected. Prompts, in the order they tend to work:

Twenty minutes ago almost nobody could write that sentence. Now almost all of you can.
And I never taught you anything about searching an array. Say it, then stop. Let them work out why. Nothing was transmitted from the front of the room – what changed is that they talked to each other.
You needed each other. Not a lecture, not a recording, not a smarter person – two people who would not accept a vague sentence.
The contract: when one of you says something fuzzy, any of the others gets to say “say that more precisely.” Not rude. The most useful thing you can say to someone trying to learn this. They will hear me say it all term.
A recording gives you information. The room gives you feedback.

Do not add an attendance pitch. They just lived the argument; saying it a second time cheapens it.
